target: pPE52IMP (GenBank CP102481.1), P. aeruginosa PE52 blaIMP-56 plasmid
note: These are truly OPEN questions — points that our sequence-only, free-tier replication could not resolve and that would require additional data, wet-lab work, or curated-database re-analysis to close.

open_questions.q: Is pPE52IMP conjugatively self-transmissible, or does it require a helper plasmid for mobilization (i.e., is the MOBP11 machinery a complete Type IV secretion system or only a relaxosome cis-acting oriT + relaxase)?
open_questions.basis: The paper annotates a MOBP11-subfamily relaxase (609 aa) and our BLASTp confirmed 100% identity to relaxases in 4 of 5 sibling plasmids. However, MOBP11 members are historically mobilizable-not-conjugative unless a full mating-pair-formation (Mpf/T4SS) apparatus is co-encoded. The 27.6 kb size of pPE52IMP is on the small end for a self-transmissible IncP-like element (typically >40 kb). Presence of traJ/traK-family gene names in the annotation does not by itself prove a functional T4SS — the annotator's substring hits could be non-functional homologs.
next_steps: Wet-lab conjugation assay: filter-mating of the PE52 donor into a plasmid-free P. aeruginosa or E. coli J53 recipient with selection on imipenem+azide; compute transfer frequency.
In silico: run oriTfinder / MOB-suite typer on CP102481.1 to classify MOB/MPF completeness rigorously and predict mobilizable-vs-conjugative status.
Compare gene inventory to a validated MOBP11 conjugative reference (e.g., RP4/RK2 IncPα backbone) to identify any missing T4SS component (virB4, virD4, trbC, etc.).

open_questions.q: What is the actual host range of the pPE52IMP replicon, and does its inability to be typed by PBRT reflect true incompatibility-group novelty or simply that PBRT's primer panel does not cover a known-but-under-represented replicon family?
open_questions.basis: The paper's PBRT non-typeability claim (C13) is a negative PCR result and is not directly verifiable from sequence alone. Our BLAST showed the RepA is 100% identical to KfrA/DNA-binding proteins in 4 sibling plasmids all restricted to P. aeruginosa hosts. This is consistent with either (a) a genuinely novel narrow-host-range replicon, or (b) an IncP-related replicon that has diverged enough in RepA to escape PBRT primers but remains functionally within a known Inc group. Distinguishing these matters for surveillance and for predicting spread to other Enterobacterales.
next_steps: Wet-lab: transform pPE52IMP into a diverse recipient panel (Pseudomonas spp., Acinetobacter baumannii, E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae) and score stable maintenance under selection.
In silico: run a curated replicon-typer such as PlasmidFinder v2 with all currently-known Pseudomonas Rep alleles and MOB-suite's rep_cluster analysis.
Search NCBI + PLSDB for all plasmids carrying a RepA identical or >95% identical to CP102481.1's 301 aa protein and tabulate host taxonomy.

open_questions.q: Is the blaIMP-56 allele call correct at the variant-specific level, and is the class-1 integron cassette architecture (intI1 → blaIMP-56 → aadA1 → blaOXA-2 → qacEΔ1 → sul1) identical to previously reported IMP-carrying integrons or does it define a new In-type?
open_questions.basis: Our replication accepted the GenBank product qualifier 'blaIMP-56' at face value (C7 confirmed only that a blaIMP-family gene is present at the right locus). IMP is a highly diverse family with >80 named alleles that can differ by single amino acids and yet produce distinct hydrolysis kinetics against carbapenems. Also, IntFinder/INTEGRALL assigns each unique integron cassette array a formal 'In' number; the paper did not report an In number for the pPE52IMP integron.
next_steps: Extract the 741-nt blaIMP CDS from CP102481.1, translate, and BLAST against the NCBI-AMR RefGene/CARD/BLDB curated β-lactamase databases to confirm the allele is IMP-56 (versus IMP-1/4/13/etc.) at the amino-acid level.
Submit the full cassette region (attI1 through qacEΔ1) to INTEGRALL for formal In-number assignment.
Compare hydrolysis-kinetics predictions (KM/kcat) with published IMP-56 characterization, if any exists.

open_questions.q: Does pPE52IMP impose a measurable fitness cost on its host, and does the presence of the intact mer operon offer a stable co-selection pressure that maintains blaIMP-56 in mercury-contaminated environments (e.g., hospital wastewater, dental amalgam, mining contexts) even in the absence of carbapenem selection?
open_questions.basis: The paper reports (and we confirmed) a complete mer operon (merRTPADE) on pPE52IMP. The classical co-selection hypothesis predicts that heavy-metal resistance stabilizes co-resident AMR determinants in environments where antibiotics are not the primary selective pressure. This is central to the epidemiology of hospital-acquired IMP-producers but was not quantified in the paper, and cannot be tested by sequence alone.
next_steps: Wet-lab: competition assays between isogenic PE52 (plasmid+) and cured PE52 (plasmid-) hosts in LB with 0/10/50 µM HgCl2 over 20 generations; measure plasmid retention frequency.
Wet-lab: minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of HgCl2 for PE52 vs plasmid-cured PE52 to confirm mer operon functionality.
Epidemiologic: query IMP-56 case reports for co-detection with mercury exposure (dental practices, mining, aquaculture) — a bioinformatic literature scan, not a wet experiment.

open_questions.q: How is pPE52IMP stably maintained through cell division in the absence of a parA/parB active-partitioning system, and is the phd/doc toxin-antitoxin the sole stability mechanism or does a hitherto-unannotated hok/sok-like or ccdA/B-like system also contribute?
open_questions.basis: The paper claims — and we confirmed — that parB is absent from pPE52IMP (C6). Yet a low-copy-number 27.6 kb plasmid without active partitioning should be lost from a lineage at every division unless a strong post-segregational-killing (PSK) or multimer-resolution mechanism compensates. The paper flags phd/doc as the stability system (C9), which we confirmed by annotation search. But phd/doc alone typically produces retention frequencies of ~99% per generation, which is marginal for the observed clinical persistence. A second, unannotated TA or a partition function homolog too diverged to be caught by qualifier-string search may also be present.
next_steps: In silico: run TAfinder and RASTA-Bacteria on the full CP102481.1 sequence to detect all TA-system candidates including cryptic ones (Type I hok/sok, Type II relBE/ccdAB, Type III toxIN).
In silico: search for parA/parM ATPase homologs by HMMER against Pfam PF01656 (CbiA / ParA) and PF06406 (ParM) — a substring search on 'parB' would miss a functional parA-only system.
Wet-lab: construct isogenic knockout of phd/doc in pPE52IMP; measure plasmid loss rate per generation in unselected culture; if loss is <1% per generation, a second stability system must exist.
